Indonesia: the rupiah falls to a record low, past 18,200 to the dollar, and the central bank must decide on Wednesday whether to defend it

On Thursday, November 12, the Indonesian rupiah fell to 18,241 to the dollar, a record low, despite interventions by Bank Indonesia. The causes: the strong dollar, bets on a Fed rate hike and MSCI's threat to remove Indonesia from its emerging-market indices. The central bank decides on its rate on November 18 [1][2][3][13].
On Thursday, November 12, the rupiah lost as much as 0.5% and hit 18,241 to the dollar, compared with 18,149 the previous evening; Reuters even noted a low of 18,243 [1][2][3].
The previous record dated from early June, at 18,190. Since January, the rupiah has lost more than 8% against the dollar: it is Asia's worst-performing currency this year [4].

Bank Indonesia says it is intervening on all fronts: rupiah forward contracts traded abroad and in Indonesia, the spot market, and purchases of government bonds; its spokesperson, Erwin Hutapea, wants the exchange rate to “reflect its fundamentals” [1][3].

The central bank cites four causes: bets on Fed rate hikes in December 2026 and in 2027, fears of a downgrade of the stock market by MSCI, the domestic economic situation and companies' year-end demand for dollars [3].

On October 15, MSCI, whose indices guide trillions of dollars in investments, proposed removing Indonesia from emerging markets and making it a “standalone market,” because of opaque shareholdings and suspected share-price manipulation [5][6].

Goldman Sachs estimates that such a downgrade would trigger about $5.6 billion in outflows from index funds [4]. MSCI's consultation runs until April 30, 2027, and the decision will come by June 30, 2027 at the latest [5].
On Friday, November 13, the Jakarta stock market rebounded 1.69% to 5,339.4 points, and the dollar was worth about 18,209 rupiah [7].

Key takeaway: Indonesia, the world's fourth most populous country, is facing both the strength of the dollar, which affects all emerging countries, and a crisis of confidence of its own, the MSCI threat [3][4].

For analysts quoted by Reuters, Bank Indonesia is partly to blame: it raised its rates more slowly than others, which makes the rupiah less attractive to investors seeking yield [4]. In October, it had left its benchmark rate at 5.75% and raised only its deposit facility rate, to 5% [14].

A weak currency makes everything Indonesia imports more expensive, starting with oil, and increases companies' dollar debts. That is Wednesday's dilemma: raise rates to defend the rupiah, at the risk of slowing an already weakened economy [2][14].

The downgrade would go far: Indonesia would jump straight from “emerging” to “standalone,” skipping the “frontier” market category. MSCI plans to go ahead unless the stock market's governance improves significantly [6][15].

If you travel to Bali, your euro goes further there than before: the rupiah has lost more than 8% against the dollar this year. On the investment side, many “emerging markets” funds hold Indonesian shares: an MSCI downgrade would force them to sell, which could weigh on their performance.

Bank Indonesia announces its rate decision at the end of a two-day meeting [13].

How it works: how a central bank defends its currency

A currency falls when more people want to sell it than buy it. When the Fed raises its rates, investing money in dollars pays more, and capital leaves emerging countries [3]. To slow the fall, a central bank has two weapons. The first: sell part of its dollar reserves and buy its own currency, directly or through forward contracts, which is what Bank Indonesia is doing [1]. But its reserves are not infinite. The second: raise its rates, so that investing money in rupiah pays more and attracts investors [4]. It is effective but costly, because credit becomes more expensive for households and businesses. An index like MSCI's also plays a role: funds that track it automatically buy or sell a country's shares depending on its category [5].
Precedents: the rupiah and its big falls
During the Asian financial crisis, the rupiah went from 2,400 to 10,000 to the dollar between July 1997 and January 1998, then to 14,000 in May 1998 [9]; it hit about 16,850 in June 1998 [10].
The Indonesian economy contracts by more than 13% and interest rates rise as high as 70% [11].
December 2014
The rupiah loses 1.9% in one session, to 12,698 to the dollar, its weakest close since August 1998 [8].
This “modern record” low would be broken several times in the following years [12][10].
September 2018
The rupiah falls to 14,750 to the dollar, its lowest since the 1998 crisis, as the Fed raises its rates [12].
In April 2020, at the start of Covid, it slides further to 15,800, close to its 1998 record [10].

Australia: Coles, one of the two supermarket giants, is investigating a cyberattack, and the stock market doesn't flinch

On Monday, November 16, Coles informed the Australian stock exchange that it was investigating a cybersecurity incident, with the help of the national cybersecurity agency. The group says it has found no evidence so far of theft of customer, employee or supplier data. Its shares gained 0.36% in early trading [1][2][3].
Coles, one of Australia's retail giants, announced on Monday that it was investigating a cybersecurity incident and informed the ASX, the Sydney stock exchange [1][2].

The group says it has identified “no evidence” that customer, employee or supplier data has been compromised or taken out of its systems; it adds that work to establish the cause and extent of the incident is continuing [2].
Coles is working with the Australian Cyber Security Centre, the federal cybersecurity agency, and with international experts tasked with “containing and securing” its IT systems [2][3].
Stores and online shopping are operating normally, as are gift cards; the group has “no indication” that accounts in the Flybuys loyalty program are affected [2].
The only reported issue: “a small number of customers” are having problems with in-store pickup at Liquorland, its liquor store chain, without Coles saying whether this is linked to the attack [2].
No hacker group has claimed the attack, and Coles has not specified which systems were targeted or how the incident was detected [2][5].
On the stock market, Coles shares were up 0.36% at 22.31 Australian dollars in early trading, while the ASX 200 index opened down 0.2% [3][4].
Key takeaway: for investors, a cyberattack is mainly costly when data is stolen. As long as Coles says it has no evidence of theft, the market waits: that is why the shares barely moved [2][3][4].

Australia has a painful memory: in 2022, health insurer Medibank first spoke of a limited incident, before acknowledging that the data of 9.7 million customers had been stolen, compared with 4 million announced at first. Its shares lost 22% [6][7].

The cost can also come from paralysis: in the United Kingdom, the April 2025 cyberattack on Marks & Spencer blocked the retailer's online orders for weeks, and the group estimated the cost at about 300 million pounds in operating profit [9].

Coles plays a big part in Australians' daily lives: together with its competitor Woolworths, it is one of the country's two major supermarket chains. An outage of checkouts or deliveries would affect millions of households; so far, nothing of the kind has been reported [1][2].

This type of attack also targets French retailers. If a store where you have an account announces a “cybersecurity incident,” change your password and be wary of emails or text messages using its name in the following days: it is hackers' first weapon, even when no data has been stolen.

How it works: what a cyberattack costs on the stock market

A listed company must notify the stock exchange of any fact that could change the value of its shares: that is why Coles published a statement to the ASX on Monday [2]. Investors then calculate three possible costs. First, the outage: blocked stores or a blocked website mean lost sales, as for Marks & Spencer in 2025 [9]. Next, data theft: it leads to investigation, legal and compensation costs and sometimes penalties, and in Australia the regulator required Medibank to set aside $167 million in additional capital [11]. Finally, customer trust, which is harder to quantify. As long as these three risks remain hypothetical, the shares move little; they fall when they are confirmed, often days later.
Precedents: three cyberattacks and their effects on the stock market
October-November 2022
Medibank reveals a hack on October 13; the number of customers affected rises from 4 to 9.7 million, and the shares lose 22% since the announcement [6][7].
On November 7, Medibank refuses to pay the ransom: the shares regain 2.3% that day, but remain 18% below their pre-attack level [8].
June 2023
The Australian banking and insurance regulator requires Medibank to set aside an extra $167 million in capital, because of the weaknesses revealed by the attack [11].
The cost of a hack is often paid months after the events, when regulators rule [11].
April-May 2025
Marks & Spencer suffers a cyberattack that blocks its online orders; the group estimates the cost at about 300 million pounds in operating profit, hoping to offset half of it [9].
In November 2025, its half-year pre-tax profit falls to 184.1 million pounds, compared with 413.1 million a year earlier, with 136 million in direct costs linked to the attack [10].

Anthropic opens its mega IPO to retail investors in Australia, Japan, Canada and part of Europe, ahead of a week in which AI faces its test

Three days before its Nasdaq debut, Anthropic, the creator of the Claude assistant, is also offering some of its shares to retail investors outside the United States, according to Market Index. The price will be set on Wednesday evening, the day after Nvidia's results: the week will show whether investors still believe in artificial intelligence [1][2].

According to the Australian stock market website Market Index, Anthropic shares are being offered to retail investors in Australia, Japan, Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland and part of Europe [1].
Anthropic is selling 825 million shares at between $70 and $78; at the top of the range, the offering would raise $64.4 billion and value the company at about $1.4 trillion [2][3].
According to CNBC, the final price is due to be set on the evening of Wednesday, November 18, for a first listing the next day, under the ticker ANT [2][4].
Seven partners, including Google and Nvidia, are also buying $26 billion of non-voting shares at the IPO price [5].
The timing is tight: Nvidia reports its results the day before, Tuesday, November 17 after the close, after losing 13% last week, its worst week since April 2025 [2].
On Sunday evening, Nasdaq-100 futures were up 0.4% and S&P 500 futures 0.1%, after a week in which the three major US indices each gained more than 2%, their best week since August [2].
The valuation has already been revised down: Anthropic was aiming for about $2 trillion in September, before the slump in AI stocks [6].

Key takeaway: this will be the biggest IPO in history, at the very moment investors are doubting AI. Opening the offering to retail investors in several countries widens the pool of buyers, at a time when every order counts [1][2][6].

The two events are linked: if Nvidia reassures on Tuesday, Anthropic could set its price at the top of the range; if it disappoints, there will be strong pressure to aim lower. Since Jensen Huang's departure on November 12, AI stocks have become very jittery [2][7].

For retail investors, nothing is guaranteed: it is the banks running the offering, led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, that allocate the shares among the requests [8], and a heavily oversubscribed IPO is often only partly filled for small investors.
History calls for caution: the biggest IPOs have sometimes started with a fall, like Facebook in 2012, and sometimes with a surge, like Saudi Aramco in 2019 [9][10][11].

If your bank or broker offers you the chance to subscribe, remember that this is not advice: the price is not yet known, the share allocated to retail investors is often reduced, and a stock can lose a lot in its first days. Even without buying any, you will feel the effect if you have a US index fund, where AI carries a lot of weight.

How it works: how an IPO price is set

Before being listed, a company tours investors (the “roadshow”) with a price range, here $70 to $78 [3]. The banks organizing the offering record orders in a “book”: how many shares each investor wants, and up to what price. If demand far exceeds supply, the final price is set at the top of the range, or even above it; otherwise, at the bottom [2]. This price is fixed the day before the first listing, here on Wednesday evening. After that, the market decides: on the first day, the stock can climb if investors who did not get shares want to buy some, or fall if demand was inflated. Retail investors go through their bank or broker, often for a reduced allocation [1][8].
Precedents: the biggest IPOs and their first steps
May 2012
Facebook raises $16 billion at $38 a share [12].
A few days later, the stock falls below its IPO price and plunges as much as 18% below it [9][10].
September 2014
Alibaba raises $25 billion in New York including the over-allotment option, a world record at the time [13].
It would take five years for that record to fall [11].
December 2019
Saudi Aramco raises $25.6 billion at 32 riyals a share, selling only about 1.5% of its capital, the record so far [11].
The stock soars on its first day of trading in Riyadh [14].

news.2026-11-16-afrique-du-sud-anc-da-ne: South Africa: the ANC and the Democratic Alliance return to the table over the big cities, with the future of the unity government in the balance

On Sunday, November 15, Cyril Ramaphosa's ANC and the Democratic Alliance (DA), its main partner in the government of national unity, opened negotiations on sharing municipal councils after the local elections. The ANC rejects a stability pact modeled on the national government, and Ramaphosa is reportedly “tired of the DA” [1][2][3].

The two parties are negotiating with other partners at the same time; according to the Daily Maverick, the ANC rules out any stability agreement with the DA on the model of the government of national unity formed in 2024 [1].
Four options have been presented to the ANC negotiating team, ranging from a unity government in the eight metros to alliances without the DA, according to Business Day [2].
The Times reports, citing internal sources, that Ramaphosa said he was “tired of the DA,” and that the ANC leadership this week called for a review of the alliance [3].
Meanwhile, Ramaphosa is in California from November 15 to 21, leading a delegation seeking investment in artificial intelligence [4].
Key takeaway: the immediate stake is the country's eight metros, and the ANC, which fell to 30.76% of the vote in the 2026 local elections, must choose its allies to govern them [2].
A break at the local level would weaken the government of national unity formed in 2024 with the DA, which the ANC leadership now wants reviewed [1][3].
A shaky coalition in Africa's leading industrial power is one more risk for the European companies that invest there, and for the economic reforms promised since 2024.
news.2026-11-16-kenya-ruto-banque-mondia: Kenya: criticized by the World Bank over corruption, William Ruto blames his predecessor and the Mombasa-Nairobi railway

On Sunday, November 15 in Narok, Kenyan President William Ruto responded to the World Bank report that names corruption as the main obstacle to the country's growth. He blames former President Uhuru Kenyatta, under whom the Mombasa-Nairobi railway (SGR) was built, cited as an example of a contract awarded without competition [1][2][3].
During a church service, Ruto said the 52-page report praised his government's reforms and asked the opposition to read it in full [1].
He declared that “some of the money funding your campaigns” could come from the SGR contracts, and pointed out that the line had been built under Uhuru Kenyatta [1][2].

Published on November 4, the report estimates that corruption costs Kenya 2% of its GDP a year, according to the World Bank's country director, Qimiao Fan, and that it may have widened the public deficit by about 2 points of GDP [4][5].
Kenya could have an economy more than 13 points larger in 2035 if it brought corruption down to the level of Ethiopia or India, according to the same study [5].
Key takeaway: with the 2027 general elections approaching, corruption is becoming the opposition's main weapon, and Ruto is trying to turn it against the former government [2][3].

According to the World Bank, corruption drives up the cost of electricity and logistics, more than twice as expensive as elsewhere, which holds back industry and jobs in East Africa's largest economy [5].
Some of the loans to Kenya come from institutions France puts money into, such as the World Bank: corruption also means development aid that gets lost along the way.
news.2026-11-16-algerie-hsbc-quitte-le-p: Algeria: British bank HSBC will leave the country after 18 years, citing a lack of profitability

HSBC Bank Middle East, the Dubai-based subsidiary of the British giant, has announced its intention to gradually close its Algiers branch, opened in 2008. The decision follows a strategic review of its corporate banking business; no closure date has been set and the Algerian press has been debating it since this weekend [1][2][3].
According to the statement, the bank wants to focus on markets where it has “a clear competitive advantage,” as part of the group's simplification [1].
The branch mainly served companies, multinationals and public bodies, not individuals; discussions with clients have begun [1][3].
HSBC says it will continue to meet its obligations to clients and the regulator until the end of the process, and will give more details “in the coming months” [1][2].
Licensed by the Bank of Algeria in June 2008, the bank had already considered leaving in 2016 but did not follow through [3].
Key takeaway: the departure of a major international bank sends a negative signal to foreign investors, just as Algiers says it wants to attract them to reduce its dependence on oil and gas [2][3].
Multinationals based in Algeria used HSBC for their international payments and trade finance: they will have to turn to other banks, often state-owned [1][3].
If you work for a French company that trades with Algeria, bank payments and guarantees could become slower or more expensive, at a time when relations between Paris and Algiers are already tense.

news.2026-11-16-australie-victoria-elect: Australia: 13 days before the Victorian state election, the ruling left promises to halve surgery waiting times, with the right the favorite

On Sunday, November 15 in Melbourne, Victoria's Labor Premier, Ben Carroll, and Liberal opposition leader Jess Wilson launched their campaigns for the November 28 election. Both promise to halve surgery waiting lists; polls show the right as the favorite, and the populist party One Nation is rising [1][2][3].
In Moonee Ponds, Carroll promised 1.17 billion Australian dollars for 100,000 extra operations in public hospitals, 30% of them in regional areas, plus 500,000 specialist consultations [2][3].
Jess Wilson's coalition also promises to halve waiting times, but by outsourcing operations to private clinics; it also wants to reopen technical schools [1][2].
A RedBridge poll conducted from November 3 to 10 puts the coalition at 31%, Labor at 23% and One Nation at 22% of voting intentions [4].

Key takeaway: Labor changed leaders in July, with Ben Carroll replacing Jacinta Allan, without recovering in the polls; a defeat would hurt the party of federal Prime Minister Anthony Albanese [1][4].
The surge of One Nation, which already finished ahead of the Liberals in the South Australian election this year, is shaking up the right; Jess Wilson refuses any debate with the party [4].
This election shows that the cost of living and access to healthcare sway voters far beyond Europe: the same issues dominate French campaigns.

The aid can reach 1,560 euros, compared with 350 euros in 2019; applications can be made until December 4 on the tax authority's myHeating platform, with a first payment before December 23 [1][2].

The offshore exploration and the cable to Cyprus aim to make Greece an energy hub in the Eastern Mediterranean [1][2].
This is a concrete example of European “energy vouchers”: France has made the same choice in recent years, at a high cost to public finances.

news.2026-11-16-nigeria-afrique-du-sud-d: Nigeria-South Africa: barely accredited, ambassador Femi Fani-Kayode falls out with the South African presidency

Nigeria's High Commission in Pretoria called for calm on Saturday, November 14 and Sunday, November 15, after Cyril Ramaphosa's spokesperson, Vincent Magwenya, accused the new Nigerian ambassador Femi Fani-Kayode of lying about an intervention by the president in a dispute over the broadcast of his accreditation ceremony [1][2][3].
During the presentation of credentials, the presidency's live broadcast cut out at the moment of Fani-Kayode's speech, which he denounced as a “deliberate” omission [2][3].
The ambassador claims that Ramaphosa apologized to him; Magwenya denies it: “There was no intervention by the president, and there never will be,” calling the move “grossly inappropriate” [2][3].
The Nigerian mission calls the spokesperson's remarks “provocative” and stands by its version, while saying it wants to preserve cordial relations [1][2].

Key takeaway: the dispute broke out just a few hours after the presentation of credentials, which is extremely rare between two partner countries; the Nigerian mission accuses the spokesperson of calling the ambassador a liar [1][2].
On the South African side, Magwenya points out that the presidency has no authority over the public broadcaster SABC [2][3].
This kind of falling-out between African heavyweights weighs on the continent's trade integration, which European companies exporting there also depend on.
